I had no luck with medication, and I simply wanted them to give me some medicine in case I suffer another attack. And in the end, I was allowed to go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was there, in your view, any direct relation between your illness and the conditions in the Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you describe what conditions, in your opinion, contributed to the inflammation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inflammation of the joints was an old complaint, and I wanted to prevent another occurrence, and I wanted to ask for the doctor in advance. But I have to tell you about the conditions that reigned there. There were 1.620 of us there at the time when I was detained there. It's an official figure. We all slept in a barn, 16 by 45 metres. During the day, and for the most time in the evenings, we were locked up and we were not allowed to go out, not even to the toilet. Instead, they would give us some barrels to use as toilet. So we were not allowed to go out at all. We lay on bare concrete, with nothing to cover ourselves or to put under our heads. Even if we wanted to turn to the other side when lying down, we were unable to do so unless everybody else turned at the same time, because we were lined up like sardines and we lived in the hope of the Red Cross coming and finding us. And this situation lasted for about two months. Two days before the Red Cross team came to take our personal details and register us, we were allowed to put some hay in the barn. We did that, and then when the Red Cross team came, they brought a blanket and a bar of soap per inmate, so that we finally had something by way of bedding and toiletries. And out of the total number of 1.620 of us, as far as I was able to count, not more than 700 people were registered. The rest were concealed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just stop you there? I asked you more specifically what conditions contributed to your health situation, and you started to describe the general conditions. I would like to know specifically -- until now you have told us about being kept inside. You've told us about hygiene. You've told us about not sufficient place and not sufficient facilities to sleep. You didn't say anything about food yet, but I'd first like to know: Was it the temperature? Was it the lack of sleep? What in the conditions contributed specifically to your inflammations, in your view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer that beatings, beatings by the guards. We were beaten, although not all of us, and in the time that I was detained there, 17 men died of beatings. None of them were killed by firearms, but solely as a consequence of beatings. People would be beaten up and then left to lie among us, and none of us were allowed to help them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you again. I am fully aware that you could tell us for a long time on the conditions in the camp, but the Prosecution has not, I would say, primarily called you in order to inform this Chamber about the conditions in the camp. Therefore, I'm specifically interested to know to what extent the camp conditions, in your case, contributed to your illness. You said beatings. Was there anything else that specifically you felt deteriorated your medical situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ-018 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you the very conditions in which we slept and the hygienic conditions, plus beatings and the food. The food was more than appalling. But under those conditions, nobody would even think of complaining. We were often left without any food at all. And even when some food was brought, the guards would toss our plates away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. That answers my questions. I'd just like to make clear to you that it is not because your experience in that camp is not of importance, but there's still a lot of witnesses to come, and since your statement mainly concerns other matters than the camp conditions, it was just briefly that I would like to know what contributed to the reasons why you were released from that camp, being sick. Did the questions of the Chamber raise any issue which needs further examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: None from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, not from the Defence either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. 018, this concludes your testimony before this Chamber. I'd like to thank you very much for coming and answering questions of all parties, although it might not have been that clear to you that you also answered the questions of the Prosecution. But of course you have given your statement and the Chamber had read that statement in advance. Thank you for coming, and I wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, you may escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to make -- to have a break and see whether later this morning or, I should say, early in the afternoon, we could perhaps have short oral argument on the submissions made. I am aware that there are some technical aspects in it. There's some case-law cited, not uncommon for common-law-trained lawyers. It's mainly, as I see from the English and the Australian cases. Whereas this Chamber, not being a Chamber -- not being a jury trial system, also very much likes to be informed about what happens in non-jury systems, because especially in the field of evidence, that sometimes gives -- I would not say another view, but an addition to the view developed in systems which are used to have jury trials. But, Mr. Hannis or Mr. Tieger, would you think that it would be of any use to perhaps reconvene at, I would say, for example, 1.00 and then spend all together perhaps 20 minutes on the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as we have just received a motion sitting here in Court, if we could have the time to look that over and inform you during this break, if we can be ready to argue this afternoon, or perhaps we can argue this afternoon with leave from the Court to file something in writing if they thought it were necessary, by the close of business. I understand the Court's desire to be able to have the argument done and decide this as soon as possible, because if Mr. Deronjic is not on Thursday, we're going to have to make some other arrangements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And since I do understand that -- tomorrow we'll sit anyhow. One of the things we could do, of course, is to have then perhaps additional oral arguments, but then not more than five to seven minutes, each party, to start with tomorrow morning, after we have received the written submission this afternoon. Would that be a way to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in principle, it's satisfactory. It certainly occurred to me when Mr. Hannis referred to written submissions, it's always desirable that there is at least some opportunity to make oral submissions on those. My nervousness about what Your Honour says is, I'm afraid, just the familiar one, is to indicate five to seven minutes in advance of having any idea of what those written submissions involve I would suggest is slightly disconcerting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I wanted to indicate, that it should be additional to what has been put on paper already. But of course I do understand that if the full German case-law would be presented by the Prosecution you might need a bit more than five to seven minutes to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm wondering whether, in the circumstances, given that -- of course I know the Tribunal is anxious to use the time today, but it does really raise the question whether it wouldn't be more satisfactory, rather than have oral submissions, with a view to it then being quite likely, it seems, that the need for written submissions and some further oral submissions, whether perhaps the timetable isn't driving us a little bit too much here and the more satisfactory way too deal with it is deal with the whole matter first thing tomorrow morning. Your Honour would no doubt have a view from the Prosecution on that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your submission has been announced already quite some time ago, and we -- I'm also aware that then the scheduling of Mr. Deronjic was not the same as it is now. But, on the other hand, it's only now on Tuesday morning that we received it. Let me just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has decided that the Prosecution will have an opportunity to briefly respond in writing this afternoon. May I take it that it could be done by 4.00? And that tomorrow a brief oral argument will be held. Whether that will be right at the beginning of the hearing or midway or at the end, that is still something to be decided. Is there anything else the parties would like to raise at this very moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Nothing from the Prosecution, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Nor from the Defence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll adjourn until 9.00 tomorrow morning, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 11th day of February 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25
